questions.prompt: A page’s content loads promptly, but text and buttons jump as images arrive. Which Core Web Vital most directly tracks the instability?

choices.text: Largest Contentful Paint as an exclusive input-latency measure.
Interaction to Next Paint as a count of network requests.
Time to First Byte as a direct score of unexpected element movement.
Cumulative Layout Shift.

questions.explanation: CLS measures visual stability. LCP concerns loading and INP interaction responsiveness; status codes do not quantify layout shift.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: Core Web Vitals use LCP for loading, INP for interaction responsiveness and CLS for visual stability.

questions.prompt: A team reports only an average LCP across every user and device. Which evidence better matches Core Web Vitals evaluation?

choices.text: Only the server’s mean response time, without page-load measurements.
A single local run treated as the complete user population.
The 75th percentile segmented by mobile and desktop.
Only the fastest measured visit in the entire sample.

questions.explanation: The guidance evaluates the 75th percentile for most users and segments device categories. A mean or best sample can hide poor experiences.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: Core Web Vitals targets are assessed at the 75th percentile with mobile and desktop segmentation; lab and field evidence are complementary.

questions.prompt: A Node.js handler performs a large synchronous computation inside an async function. What remains a risk?

choices.text: Each HTTP request gets an independent JavaScript event loop.
The computation can block the event loop.
The async keyword automatically sends all CPU work to a worker thread.
Promises guarantee every callback takes constant time.

questions.explanation: Async syntax does not relocate synchronous CPU work. A long callback can delay other requests on the event loop.

sources.title: Do not block the Event Loop
sources.claim: Node.js uses an event loop and worker pool; long synchronous callbacks block other work, and wrapping CPU work in async syntax does not move it off the loop.

questions.prompt: A slow page’s trace shows most server time inside one downstream call. Which next investigation follows the evidence?

choices.text: Inspect that dependency span and compare browser timing boundaries.
Rewrite CSS first because all slow pages are layout problems.
Increase server instances without checking the dependency limit.
Remove timing instrumentation once the response returns 200.

questions.explanation: Trace timing localizes server work and browser entries locate user-facing phases. A status or arbitrary rewrite does not identify the bottleneck.

sources.title: Performance API
sources.claim: Browser performance entries and distributed trace spans provide timing evidence at different boundaries, supporting localization rather than guessing a bottleneck.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry traces
sources.claim: Browser performance entries and distributed trace spans provide timing evidence at different boundaries, supporting localization rather than guessing a bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A page’s loading score improves but interaction responsiveness worsens. Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: All Core Web Vitals must improve by the same proportion.
INP becomes irrelevant whenever the first content loads quickly.
A good loading metric proves no long interaction tasks exist.
LCP improvement does not guarantee INP improvement.

questions.explanation: Core Web Vitals cover different experience dimensions. Improving loading alone does not establish responsive interactions.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: LCP measures loading, INP responsiveness and CLS stability rather than interchangeable qualities.

questions.prompt: A local lab test is fast, but field measurements are slow on mobile visits. What should the investigation preserve?

choices.text: Only the fastest mobile observation as the release decision.
One combined average that discards device and population differences.
Both datasets and their different populations and conditions.
Only the lab result because it invalidates all user measurements.

questions.explanation: Lab and field data answer different questions. Keeping their context helps diagnose variation rather than discarding evidence.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: Field measurements reflect actual users while lab measurements use controlled conditions.

questions.prompt: Which Core Web Vital mappings are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: INP reflects interaction responsiveness.
CLS measures server database transaction duration.
INP is the cumulative amount of page layout movement.
LCP is a guarantee that all later interactions will be responsive.
LCP reflects loading performance of prominent content.

questions.explanation: A is correct: It concerns the next visual response to interactions. B is incorrect: It measures visual layout instability. C is incorrect: That describes the domain of CLS. D is incorrect: Loading and interaction performance are separate dimensions. E is correct: It measures when the largest contentful element is painted.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: Core Web Vitals use LCP for loading, INP for interaction responsiveness and CLS for visual stability.

questions.prompt: Which measurement practices fit user-experience assessment? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assess Core Web Vitals targets at the 75th percentile.
Assume one fast local visit proves every real user meets the targets.
Combine every device category and ignore mobile performance differences.
Use real-user field data to understand experienced performance.
Use lab tests to reproduce and investigate controlled conditions.

questions.explanation: A is correct: This is the documented evaluation threshold. B is incorrect: A local sample does not represent the full population. C is incorrect: The guidance calls for mobile and desktop segmentation. D is correct: Field measurements reflect actual visits. E is correct: They complement field evidence.

sources.title: Web Vitals
sources.claim: Core Web Vitals targets are assessed at the 75th percentile with mobile and desktop segmentation; lab and field evidence are complementary.

questions.prompt: Which statements guide Node.js performance diagnosis? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Treat a Promise wrapper as automatic CPU-work offloading.
Use request isolation as proof that one callback cannot affect other clients.
Keep event-loop callbacks short enough to preserve responsiveness.
A synchronous API can block the event loop despite an async function wrapper.
Assume all filesystem and cryptographic operations share identical scheduling behavior.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Wrapping a computation does not move it to another thread. B is incorrect: Clients share event-loop execution time. C is correct: Long callbacks delay unrelated work. D is correct: The function declaration does not change that work’s execution. E is incorrect: Some use the worker pool while synchronous variants block.

sources.title: Do not block the Event Loop
sources.claim: Node.js uses an event loop and worker pool; long synchronous callbacks block other work, and wrapping CPU work in async syntax does not move it off the loop.

questions.prompt: Which evidence helps diagnose a slow full-stack request? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume the longest visible page load phase must be database execution.
Use browser performance entries to inspect user-facing timing.
Use related trace spans to inspect server and dependency work.
Compare timings before and after a targeted change.
Treat HTTP 200 as proof that user-visible latency is acceptable.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Browser and server boundaries require correlation. B is correct: They expose browser-side operation measurements. C is correct: Span timing locates time within the distributed operation. D is correct: Measurement establishes whether the suspected cause improved. E is incorrect: Successful status says nothing about responsiveness.
